hypothesis.title: The First Cut Listens
hypothesis.question: Does changing the front-end representation of the same musical passage change which musical relations survive downstream processing?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If the same passage is routed through Bark-band, phase-aware, compressed-audio, and symbolic-score front ends, then listeners will report different survival patterns for masking clarity, groove coherence, timbral identity, and notated structure, because each representation preserves and discards different relations before interpretation begins.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: The selected sources converge on front-end representation as a causal musical variable. Bark-scale dynamics aligns processing bands with psychoacoustic critical-band structure rather than arbitrary crossovers [S1]. StreamMark shows that complex-domain audio representations can carry imperceptible identity markers through benign transformations while failing under semantics-altering manipulation [S3]. PHALAR reports that pitch-equivariant and phase-equivariant representations improve stem retrieval and correlate better with human musical coherence judgments than phase-discarding baselines [S4]. Speech-recognition fairness results identify audio encoder design and compression quality as stronger levers for robustness and accent fairness than LLM scale [S5]. MSU-Bench finds modality gaps between ABC and PDF score understanding, implying that symbolic and visual score front ends expose different musical facts [S6]. The ice-phase source supplies a physical analogy: possible structures are constrained by accessible pathways, not just abstract validity [S2].

recipe.title: First-Cut Etudes
recipe.bodyMd: Compose one 60-second passage, then render it through four front ends while keeping the musical material constant: same tempo, harmonic skeleton, rhythm, and stems. First, make a Bark-band version with 24 Bark-aligned or Bark-approximated dynamics/EQ groups to test whether masking-sensitive separation improves [S1]. Second, make a phase-aware version that preserves stereo phase, transients, and microtiming while minimizing magnitude edits, then judge stem coherence [S4]. Third, make a compressed-encoder version using low-bitrate or bandwidth-limited export and identify which accent, articulation, or timbral cues disappear first [S5]. Fourth, translate the material into ABC or another sparse symbolic score and reconstruct it, noting what survives notation and what needed visual, timbral, or performance context [S6]. Add a barely audible hidden marker inspired by StreamMark that should survive benign processing but vanish under one chosen destructive transform [S3]. The expected result is not one best render, but a map of which representation makes each musical relation reachable, echoing the path-dependent accessibility of physical phase formation [S2].
dawChecklist: Create a 60-second passage with separate stems and a fixed harmonic/rhythmic skeleton.
Render a control mix with no special front-end treatment.
Render a Bark-band version using 24 Bark-aligned or approximate critical-band EQ/dynamics regions.
Render a phase-aware version that preserves transient placement, stereo phase, and microtiming.
Render a compressed-encoder version at a deliberately low bitrate or restricted bandwidth.
Export a sparse symbolic score representation such as ABC, then reconstruct audio from it.
Embed one barely audible rhythmic or spectral marker and apply one destructive transform intended to erase it.
Rate each render from 1 to 5 for harmonic function, groove coherence, timbral identity, and hidden-marker survival.
Treat equal ratings across all renders as disconfirming evidence that front-end choice mattered for this passage.

protocol.listeningContext: Studio monitors or neutral headphones; compare loudness-matched renders against the untreated control.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind or shuffled A/B/C/D comparison followed by 1-5 survival ratings on four axes.
